Before there were graves, the trees bore names instead of fruit, and each name belonged to someone not yet born. A child wandered among them, listening for her own. When she found it trembling on a low branch, she reached up and plucked it. At once her mother, far away beside the river, forgot how to breathe. Thus death entered the world, not as a hunter, but as a silence between two calls.

The tree bent until its leaves touched the child’s hair. “I am sorry,” it said, and dropped its remaining names into the earth. Wherever they fell, white roots curled around the dead, holding them gently against the dark. But the child would not forgive it. She carried her mother’s name through every season, until it softened in her palm and became the first pear. This is why fruit tastes sweetest just before it spoils, and why the orchard is grey at dawn.
